questions.question: In operations research, which description fits a heuristic, the kind of solution method whose solutions must satisfy all constraints of the original problem?
options: A method seeking a good feasible solution without a guarantee of optimality
A method that always finds an optimal solution, only faster than exact ones
A method that may return infeasible plans whenever they score better
A method that gives a bound on the optimal value but no actual solution

questions.question: A quick planning method returns a production plan that exceeds the available machine hours by 5% but earns more than any plan that respects the hours. Is this an acceptable heuristic solution, given that heuristic solutions must satisfy the original constraints?
options: Yes; heuristics may bend constraints slightly to reach better plans.
Yes, as long as the 5% violation is reported together with the plan.
No; a heuristic solution must satisfy all the original constraints.
Yes, and its profit is a valid lower bound on the best profit.

questions.question: For a profit-maximization problem with optimal value $z^*$, a heuristic returns a feasible plan with profit 340. Why does this give $z^*\ge340$?
options: Heuristics aim low on purpose, so their values stay below the optimum.
The optimum is at least as good as every feasible plan, this one too.
The heuristic ignores some constraints, which can only lower its profit.
It does not; a feasible profit is an upper bound on $z^*$ instead.

questions.question: A firm can fund any subset of a few projects within a budget and wants the largest total return. Which solution method for this selection problem is a heuristic rather than an exact method?
options: Listing every subset of projects within the budget and keeping the best one
Checking whether a proposed selection of projects stays within the budget
Each time adding the project with the highest return that still fits
Computing each project's return per unit of cost and ranking the projects

questions.question: A planner must decide whether to use a heuristic, a method that gives a good feasible solution without guaranteeing optimality. In which situation is a heuristic most appropriate?
options: When the plan must come with a proof that no better feasible plan exists
When an exact optimum would take too long and a good feasible plan is needed soon
When some constraints may be loosened a little to obtain a better objective value
When the problem is tiny, so that every plan can be compared in a few seconds

questions.question: A knapsack holds at most 10 kg. Items have weight and value P (5 kg, 10), Q (4 kg, 7), R (3 kg, 6) and S (3 kg, 5). A heuristic considers items in order of decreasing value and adds each one that still fits. What total value does it obtain?
For a cost-minimization problem with optimal value $z^*$, a heuristic returns a plan that satisfies every constraint and costs 52. What can be concluded about $z^*$?

10 units must be bought. Supplier A charges a fee of 10 if used plus 3 per unit, for at most 6 units; supplier B charges a fee of 2 if used plus 4 per unit, for at most 10 units. A heuristic buys as much as possible from the lowest unit price first. What does its plan cost?

A tour must start at town A, visit B, C and D once each and return to A. Distances: AB 2, AC 3, AD 4, BC 6, BD 1, CD 5. The nearest-neighbour heuristic always moves to the closest unvisited town. What is the length of its tour?
For a cost-minimization problem, a heuristic finds a plan that satisfies every constraint and costs 52. A colleague's method, claimed to be exact, reports an optimal cost of 55. What follows?
options: 55 cannot be the optimal cost, since a feasible plan costing only 52 exists.
The heuristic plan must be infeasible, as heuristics cannot beat exact methods.
Both can be right, since heuristics and exact methods measure different costs.
The optimal cost is exactly 52, since the heuristic beat the exact method.

questions.question: A heuristic for a cost-minimization problem returns a feasible plan costing 45, and nothing else is known about the problem's optimal cost. How far is this plan from optimal?
options: At most 10% above the optimum, which is the usual accuracy of a heuristic.
Not at all; a heuristic's plan is optimal unless shown to be otherwise.
Unknown: it may be optimal or far from it; a bound from below is needed.
Strictly above the optimum, since a heuristic never finds an optimal plan.

questions.question: On one problem instance, a greedy heuristic returns a plan that complete enumeration confirms to be optimal. Does this make the greedy rule an exact method?
options: Yes; a method whose output was shown to be optimal is an exact method.
Yes, provided it also ran faster than the complete enumeration did.
No, since a plan found by a heuristic can never actually be optimal.
No; on other instances it may do worse, lacking a general guarantee.

questions.question: For a cost-minimization problem with optimal value $z^*$, plan X violates a capacity constraint and costs 40, while the best heuristic plan, which satisfies all constraints, costs 45. What does the cost 40 of plan X tell us about $z^*$?
options: $z^*\le40$, since 40 is the lowest cost found by any plan so far.
Nothing; only plans that meet every constraint give a valid bound.
$z^*\ge40$, since infeasible plans are always the cheaper ones.
$z^*=40$, once the violated capacity constraint is repaired.

questions.question: 10 units must be bought: supplier A has a fee of 10 if used plus 3 per unit for at most 6 units, and supplier B a fee of 2 if used plus 4 per unit for at most 10 units. Buying from the lowest unit price first gives A 6 units and B 4 units, costing 46. Is this plan optimal?
options: Yes; buying the cheapest units first is always best
No; buying all 10 units from A costs only 40
No; buying all 10 units from B costs only 42
Yes; moving one unit to B raises the cost to 47

questions.question: Four towns have distances AB 1, AC 2, AD 5, BC 3, BD 4, CD 6. A tour starts and ends at A and visits each other town once. Nearest neighbour from A gives A, B, C, D, A with length 15. What does comparing it with the other tours show?
options: Tour A, B, D, C, A has length 13, so nearest neighbour is not optimal.
Nearest neighbour is optimal, since every move goes to the closest town.
Reversing the tour to A, D, C, B, A shortens it to 13 kilometres.
Every tour has length 15, since each town is visited exactly once.

questions.question: Jobs of 5, 4, 3, 3 and 3 hours must be split over two machines to finish all work as early as possible. A heuristic takes the jobs from longest to shortest and gives each to the machine with less work so far (machine 1 on a tie). When does its schedule finish, and is it optimal?
options: At 10; not optimal, since $\{5,4\}$ and $\{3,3,3\}$ end at 9
At 10; optimal, as the longest jobs are always placed first
At 9; the rule always balances the two machine loads exactly
At 8, the time at which machine 1 finishes its last job

questions.question: A heuristic starts from a feasible plan and repeatedly makes a single change that keeps the plan feasible and improves the objective; it stops when no such single change exists. What can be said about the final plan?
options: It is feasible, but a plan needing several changes at once may be better.
It is optimal, since no improving change is left anywhere in the problem.
It is optimal, provided the starting plan already satisfied all constraints.
It may be infeasible, since the changes are made one at a time.

questions.question: For a cost-minimization problem, heuristic H1 returns a feasible plan costing 48 and heuristic H2 a feasible plan costing 45. Nothing else is known. What can be concluded about optimality?
options: H2's plan is optimal, being the better of the two heuristic plans.
H1's plan is certainly not optimal; H2's plan may or may not be.
Both plans could be optimal, since heuristics only estimate costs.
Neither plan can be judged until a lower bound is available.

questions.question: A knapsack holds at most 12 kg; items A (7 kg, value 10), B (6 kg, 8), C (6 kg, 8), D (5 kg, 4). Greedy-by-value packs A and D (value 14). No exchange of one packed item for one unpacked item gives a feasible packing of higher value. Is A and D optimal?
options: Yes; no single exchange improves it, so it is optimal.
Yes; greedy by value is optimal when weights are whole kilograms.
No; A, B and D are together worth 22.
No; B and C together weigh 12 kg and are worth 16.

questions.question: For maximize $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+2x_2\le8$, $3x_1+x_2\le9$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, a heuristic sets $x_2=0$ and makes $x_1$ as large as possible, giving $(3,0)$ with value 3. A planner concludes that no feasible plan exceeds 3. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The claim holds, because the heuristic plan satisfies every constraint.
The claim holds unless the heuristic broke one of the two constraints.
Only $z^*\ge3$; the feasible point $(2,3)$ gives 5, so the claim fails.
$z^*\le3$, which a better heuristic could later raise above 3.
